title: Characters, ASCII, Unicode and Data Units
intro: Catch up with the essential learning in about 10–15 minutes. Complete five short steps and check your answers as you go.

stages.label: Remember
stages.lead: Start with two questions from the previous lesson.

stages.label: Learn
stages.lead: Read these three short explanations. They contain the essential knowledge.

blocks.title: Characters are stored as numbers
blocks.text: A character set maps each character to a number. These numbers can be represented in binary. For example, uppercase A has ASCII code 65, represented as 01000001 in eight bits; B has code 66, represented as 01000010.

blocks.title: ASCII and Unicode
blocks.text: Standard ASCII covers a relatively small set of characters. Unicode covers many more languages and symbols. Unicode can use different encodings; a character does not always use one byte.

blocks.title: Worked example
blocks.text: 12 characters × 8 bits = 96 bits. 96 ÷ 8 = 12 bytes. This assumes exactly 8 bits per character and ignores file headers.

questions.prompt: What is the ASCII code for uppercase A in our example?
Which statement about Unicode is accurate?
options: It supports fewer symbols than ASCII
It supports more languages and writing systems
Every character uses exactly one byte
questions.answer: It supports more languages and writing systems
questions.feedback: Unicode supports far more characters. The number of bytes depends on the encoding and character.

questions.prompt: How many bits are in a nibble?

stages.label: Practise
stages.lead: Use quick matching, ordering and calculations to secure the ideas.

blocks.text: For a text-size calculation, multiply the number of characters by bits per character, then divide by 8 for bytes.

questions.prompt: Match each uppercase character to the correct ASCII code.
questions.feedback: A = 65, B = 66 and C = 67. Codes distinguish the characters.

questions.prompt: Put the stages of storing the character B in the correct order.
How many bits are in one byte?
A message has 12 characters. Each uses exactly 8 bits. How many bytes is the text?

stages.label: Apply
stages.lead: Code First, then one exam-style explanation. The written response is self-checked, not given an unreliable automatic mark.

blocks.title: Code First · Predict → Write → Test → Improve
blocks.caption: Predict the output. Then change the assignment to 66 and predict again.

blocks.text: Exam-style writing: Explain one advantage of Unicode over ASCII, and why you cannot assume that every Unicode character uses one byte.

questions.prompt: What number does the original program print?
questions.feedback: It prints the numeric value of characterCode, which starts as 65.

questions.prompt: After changing the assignment to 66, what number is printed?
questions.feedback: The variable is now 66. Printing its number does not automatically print the letter B.

questions.prompt: 80 characters use 16 bits each. How many bytes of raw character data is that?

writing.prompt: Write two or three sentences answering the exam-style question.
writing.model: Unicode supports a much wider range of characters and writing systems than ASCII, allowing more languages and symbols to be represented. Unicode has different encodings, and some characters may use multiple bytes, so one byte per character is not always correct.
checklist: I explained that Unicode represents more characters and languages than ASCII.
I explained that Unicode characters can use different numbers of bytes.
I compared my explanation with the model answer and corrected anything missing.

stages.label: Check
stages.lead: Three final statements, then review your whole-lesson score.

questions.feedback: True: one byte is eight bits.

questions.prompt: Unicode is limited to fewer characters than standard ASCII.
questions.feedback: False: Unicode covers a much wider repertoire.

questions.prompt: Every Unicode character always occupies exactly one byte.
questions.feedback: False: it depends on the encoding and the character.
